episode_title: Inside the Wired Pod Project: How 24 Women Raised $1 Million for Commercial Real Estate

real_qa.q: How much equity did 24 women investors raise for the Pod Project through Wired and what was the timeline from pitch to closing?
real_qa.r: The group raised right at one million dollars from 24 total investors, all female, some of whom had no prior commercial real estate ownership experience. They started pursuing the project at the beginning of March and closed on July 10th, completing the fundraising in approximately four months.
real_qa.requete: Pod Project Wired women 24 investors million dollars

real_qa.q: What is the history and origin of the Pod Project building at 6330 Lamar, and why is it called the Pod Project?
real_qa.r: The building was built in 1969 at 6330 Lamar as a TWA Breech Academy campus where stewardesses from around the country attended six to eight week training programs. It consisted of dormitories, each with a different country theme and sunken living rooms. The project is called the Pod Project because from an aerial view, the five different offshoots of the building look like pods.
real_qa.requete: Pod Project 6330 Lamar TWA building history

real_qa.q: What role does the pro forma play in developing a commercial real estate investment opportunity like the Pod Project?
real_qa.r: Katie Ramos views the pro forma as a living, breathing document and silent teammate in the investment process. She notes that every pro forma is wrong because projections are liable to change, so the team works to make as many accurate projections as possible while remaining flexible as circumstances evolve. The pro forma must be refined to a presentable state that paints a clear financial picture before building everything else around it.
real_qa.requete: pro forma commercial real estate investment document

real_qa.q: What due diligence process did the sponsorship team use to evaluate the Pod Project before pitching it to Wired investors?
real_qa.r: The sponsorship team of four—Cheryl Vickers, Katie Ramos, Heather Luce, and attorney Danielle Wallace—conducted heavy due diligence by turning over every stone during inspection, asking as many questions as possible, and leaving no stone unturned until they felt confident enough to move forward. The inclusion of an attorney from the start was identified as a game-changing decision.
real_qa.requete: commercial real estate due diligence sponsorship team

real_qa.q: What advice does Katie Ramos give to women entering commercial real estate investment for the first time?
real_qa.r: Ramos emphasizes the importance of understanding pro formas and key financial documents, learning from experienced developers and partners in group investment structures, and viewing challenges as growth opportunities. She advocates for a 1% better every day mindset and staying poised when facing skepticism, as she experienced early in her career when someone asked if she was at a meeting with her dad rather than as a broker.
real_qa.requete: women commercial real estate first investment advice

guest.bio_context: Katie Ramos is a Kansas City native who started her career with the Kansas City Royals in 2015 before transitioning to commercial real estate at DLM Commercial, where she was mentored by founders Otto Westerfeld and Alan Bischoff. She became a partner at DLM Commercial Real Estate Services and DLM Property Management, and currently serves as Investment Chair for Wired, leading deal evaluation and sponsorship for group investment opportunities.
